## Use of Low Memory ($0000–$03FF)

BASIC uses the [low memory area](./memory/low-memory-map.md) for program management, variable tracking, and floating-point math, with temporary overlap of certain KERNAL variables. It shares this space with the Kernal.

| Range | Purpose | Key Variables / Pointers |
|:------|:---------|:-------------------------|
| `$002B–$0030` | Core pointers defining BASIC memory layout | TXTTAB, VARTAB, ARYTAB |
| `$0031–$0038` | Free-space and string pool boundaries | STREND, FREETOP, MEMSIZ |
| `$0039–$0042` | Current/previous line context and DATA pointer | CURLIN, OLDLIN, DATPTR |
| `$0061–$006E` | Floating point accumulators (FAC1/FAC2) | FP math workspace |
| `$0073–$007A` | Inline copy of CHRGET/CHRGOT tokenizer entry | BASIC text reader |
| `$0099–$009A` | Default I/O device numbers | DFLTN (input), DFLTO (output) |
| `$0200–$0258` | Input buffer for keyboard and direct statements | INBUF |
| `$0281–$0284` | BASIC start and end addresses after memory test | BASBOT, BASTOP |
| `$0300–$030B` | **BASIC RAM vectors** (redirectable entry points) | e.g. LIST, NEW, RUN |
| `$033C–$03FB` | Cassette buffer reused by BASIC LOAD/SAVE | TBUFFER |

BASIC and KERNAL share portions of this map; modifying these variables directly  
allows the relocation of program text, redefining top-of-memory, or injecting custom LOAD/SAVE behavior.

## Use of Low Memory ($0000–$03FF)

The KERNAL relies on the [low memory region](./memory/low-memory-map.md) for all I/O and interrupt control. It shares this space with BASIC.

| Range | Purpose | Key Variables / Vectors |
|:------|:---------|:------------------------|
| `$0000–$0001` | 6510 I/O registers controlling memory banking and cassette motor | D6510, R6510 |
| `$0090` | I/O **status byte** updated by KERNAL routines | STATUS |
| `$009B–$00A2` | System clock and **TIME** variables for RDTIM/SETTIM | TI, TI$ |
| `$00B8–$00BC` | File/device association (LFN, SA, FA) | LA, SA, FA, FNADR |
| `$00C6` | Keyboard buffer count | NDX |
| `$00F3–$00F6` | Vectors to color RAM and keyboard decode tables | USER, KEYTAB |
| `$0314–$0333` | **Interrupt and I/O vectors** (modifiable by user) | CINV, CBINV, IRQ, BRK, NMI, etc. |
| `$033C–$03FB` | **Cassette buffer** (192 bytes, reusable for ML code if no tape is used) | TBUFFER |
| `$03FC–$03FF` | Unused bytes (safe for temporary data) | — |

The KERNAL modifies `$0001` to switch ROM/RAM banks, writes device status to `$0090`,  
and maintains IRQ/NMI linkage through `$0314–$0318`. Avoid overwriting these unless intercepting system vectors.

### Display Text on Screen

1) KERNAL CHROUT (portable)
   - Put PETSCII byte in A; JSR $FFD2 to print at cursor. Handles charset mapping.
   - Use for portability and when charset may vary.
2) Direct screen writes (fast)
   - STA $0400,X writes VIC-II screen codes directly. Use when you control charset and need speed.
   - Color via STA $D800,X (4-bit color index).

Screen-code conversion

- If input is ASCII uppercase 'A'..'Z', convert: screen = PETSCII - $40 (e.g. $41→$01). Implement in a small loop if needed.

This file is intentionally minimal: use `src/tools/basicTokenizer.ts` / `src/tools/assembler.ts` for tokenization/PRG building and `data/graphics/character-set.csv` for exact screen-code mappings.

# C64 Knowledge Bootstrap

High-level overview for C64 development. For more details, see linked spec documents.

## Backend Selection

Two backends may be available: `c64u` (physical C64 Ultimate hardware) and `vice`
(VICE emulator). Use `c64_select_backend` to switch.

**Routing rules — call `c64_select_backend` first when the user:**
- Says "use vice", "on vice", "in the emulator", "via vice", or similar
- Says "use c64u", "on hardware", "on the Ultimate", "on the real machine", or similar
- Prefixes a request with a backend name, e.g. "vice: run this program"

Do not assume the current backend is correct without checking
`c64://platform/status` if the user has expressed a preference.

## Fast Paths

- Game development: read `c64://gamedev/index` first (modern Ultimate by default, or stock C64); route to `.github/skills/game-development/SKILL.md`.
- Grouped MCP tools are never called bare. For tools such as `c64_program`, `c64_memory`, `c64_graphics`, `c64_sound`, and `c64_system`, call the tool with flat arguments that include `op`.
- Wrong: `c64_program {}` or `{ "c64_program": { "op": "cross_platform_greeting" } }`. Correct: call tool `c64_program` with `{ "op": "cross_platform_greeting" }`.
- For simple visible confirmation on `vice`, `c64u`, or both, prefer `c64_program` with `op: "cross_platform_greeting"`.
- For trivial hello-world and smoke-test requests, route to `.github/skills/hello-world/SKILL.md` and let that skill use the shortest greeting workflow.
- That workflow switches backends internally, writes a platform-customized BASIC greeting, captures screenshots, and verifies the rendered text without extra tool composition.
- Use manual `c64_select_backend` with `op: "select"` plus `c64_program` with `op: "upload_run_basic"` only when the user needs custom program logic beyond a quick greeting or text demo.
- On local machines with a graphical session, assume VICE should be visible by default. Only expect Xvfb or other headless fallback in CI or when no framebuffer/display session exists.
- For manual visible VICE BASIC runs, avoid immediate `read_screen` or `wait_for_text` calls, because Binary Monitor traffic traps execution while servicing requests.

## Device & Services

- MCP server controls Ultimate 64/C64 via REST: upload/run BASIC or ASM, screen/memory I/O, drives, SID music, audio analysis, local RAG.
- Key chips: VIC-II ($D000), SID ($D400), CIA1 ($DC00), CIA2 ($DD00).

## Memory Map (default RAM layout)

For full details see `../memory/memory-map.md`. Use `../memory/low-memory-map.md` for zero page/pages 0-3, `../basic/rom-routines.md` for BASIC ROM routines, `../kernal/rom-routines.md` for KERNAL ROM routines, and `../io/io-spec.md` or `../io/cia-spec.md` for hardware registers.

- $0000–$00FF: Zero page
- $0100–$01FF: Stack
- $0200–$02FF: Workspace, vectors ($0314/$0315 IRQ, $0318/$0319 BRK)
- $0400–$07E7: Screen RAM (text 40×25)
- $0801–: BASIC program area (defaults)
- $A000–$BFFF: BASIC ROM (banked; RAM when LORAM/HIRAM cleared)
- $C000–$CFFF: RAM (common for ASM)
- $D000–$DFFF: I/O area (VIC-II $D000–$D02E; SID $D400–$D418; Color RAM $D800–$DBE7; CIA1/2 $DC00/$DD00)
- $E000–$FFFF: KERNAL ROM (banked)

Bank control (6510 at $0001):

- Bits: 0 LORAM, 1 HIRAM, 2 CHAREN. Typical full RAM: %0000_0011 → clear for RAM, set for ROM.

## Video (VIC-II)

The VIC-II chip handles graphics and sprites. Fore more information see `data/graphics/vic-spec.md`.

- Sprites: X ($D000..$D00E even), Y ($D001..$D00F odd), X MSBs $D010.
- Control: $D011 (bit 7: 25th row; bit 6: RST8; bit 5: bitmap on; bits 0–2: vertical scroll).
- Raster line: $D012 (LSB), $D011 bit 7 forms MSB; raster IRQ: mask $D01A, status $D019, vector $0314/$0315.
- Control 2/Multicolour: $D016 (bit 4: 38/40 cols; bit 5: multicolour; bits 0–2: horizontal scroll).
- Memory pointers: $D018 (bits 1–3: screen base; bits 4–7: charset/bitmap base).
- Sprite enable: $D015; expand X: $D01D; expand Y: $D017; priority: $D01B; multicolour: $D01C.
- Colors: Border $D020; background 0–3 $D021–$D023; sprite multicolour $D025–$D026; sprite colours $D027–$D02E.
- Collisions: sprite-sprite $D01E (read/clear by write); sprite-background $D01F.

Video modes:

- Text: $D011 bit 5=0; $D016 bit 5=0 (hi-res); charset and screen from $D018.
- Bitmap: $D011 bit 5=1; hi-res (single colour per 8×8) or multicolour ($D016 bit 5=1).
- Multicolour text/bitmap: wide pixels using $D022–$D024 and colour RAM.

Bitmap setup (typical):

- Screen map at $0400 ($D018 bits 1–3 = 1), bitmap at $2000 ($D018 bits 4–7 = 8).
- Enable bitmap: set $D011 bit 5; optional multicolour: set $D016 bit 5.

### PETSCII, Screen & Colors

- Screen at $0400 (40×25); write screen codes. Colour RAM at $D800 (nybbles). Border $D020, background $D021.
- To draw pixels: use bitmap mode and write to bitmap memory; control colours via attributes (screen/colour RAM in text, nybbles per cell in bitmap multicolour).

### PETSCII String Pitfalls

- PETSCII is not ASCII: characters such as the backslash map to control codes (e.g. `$1C` toggles reverse video in the default upper/graphics set). Switch to the lower/upper character set first (`CHR$(14)` or `POKE 53272,14`) or pick alternative glyphs if you need a literal `\` on screen.
- Commodore BASIC does not interpret `\n` as a newline. When emitting multi-line art, either print each line separately or inject carriage returns explicitly with `CHR$(13)`.

Example:

```basic
10 PRINT CHR$(147);CHR$(14);" /\\_/\\"
20 PRINT " ( o.o )"
30 PRINT "  > ^ <"
40 PRINT CHR$(142)
```

## Raster IRQ Setup

Use this to trigger code at a specific raster line, e.g. for split-screen effects, multiplexing sprites, or scrolling in the border without screen tear.

1. Disable interrupts: `SEI`.
2. Set raster line `$D012`, configure `$D011` bit 7 accordingly.
3. Set IRQ vector `$0314/$0315` to handler.
4. Enable IRQ in `$D01A` and global `CLI`.
5. In handler: do work (e.g., change colours/sprites), then `LDA $D019`/`STA $D019` to clear and `RTI`.

## Image & Sprites

- Bitmap (hi-res): set `$D011` bit 5=1, `$D016` bit 5=0; point `$D018` to screen/bitmap; write bits into bitmap memory.
- Multicolour bitmap: also set `$D016` bit 5=1; use `$D022–$D024` and colour RAM per cell.
- Sprites: define 63-byte patterns; set sprite pointers at $07F8–$07FF; position with `$D000–$D00F`, enable with `$D015`.

## Audio (SID)

The SID chip handles audio synthesis. For more information see `data/sound/sid-spec.md`.

Per voice (1..3; base offsets +0x07 per voice):

- FREQ LO/HI: $D400/$D401, $D407/$D408, $D40E/$D40F.
- PULSE LO/HI: $D402/$D403, $D409/$D40A, $D410/$D411.
- CONTROL: $D404, $D40B, $D412 (bit 0 GATE; 1 SYNC; 2 RING; 3 TEST; 4 TRI; 5 SAW; 6 PULSE; 7 NOISE).
- ADSR: $D405 (A hi-nibble, D lo-nibble), $D406 (S hi-nibble, R lo-nibble).

Filter/Master:

- Cutoff: $D415/$D416; resonance/voice routing: $D417; volume/filter mode: $D418 (low 4 bits volume 0–15; bits 4–7 filter + third-voice mute).

Making sound (basic):

1. Set frequency ($D400/01).
2. Set pulse width ($D402/03) if pulse.
3. Set ADSR ($D405/06).
4. Set waveform + GATE in CONTROL ($D404).
5. Set master volume at $D418.

## BASIC

Basic is used for simple programs and quick prototyping. It is very slow compared to assembly. For more information see `data/basic/basic-spec.md`.

- Program: numbered lines; end with `END` or stop on last line.
- Variables: A–Z (and arrays A()(numeric), A$() string); strings end with `$`.
- Assignment: `LET A=expr` (LET optional) | `A$="TEXT"`.
- I/O: `PRINT expr[,;expr...]` | `INPUT var` | `GET A$` | `OPEN ch,dev,sa,"name"` | `PRINT#ch,expr` | `CLOSE ch`.
- Control: `IF expr THEN <stmt|line>` | `GOTO n` | `GOSUB n` | `RETURN` | `FOR v=start TO end STEP s: ... : NEXT v` | `ON x GOTO l1,...` | `ON x GOSUB l1,...`.
- Data: `DATA v1,v2,...` | `READ var` | `RESTORE`.
- System: `POKE addr,val` | `PEEK(addr)` | `SYS addr` | `RUN` | `STOP` | `NEW`.
- Strings: `LEFT$(s,n)` `RIGHT$(s,n)` `MID$(s,p[,n])` `CHR$(n)` `ASC(s)` `LEN(s)`.
- Math: `+ - * / ^` | `ABS` `INT` `SGN` `SQR` `SIN` `COS` `TAN` `ATN` `RND([n])` `FRE(0)` `TI$`.
- Relational: `= <> < > <= >=` (boolean as -1/0).
- Remarks: `REM text` (tokens ignored till end of line).
- Example (print to printer device 4): `OPEN 4,4:PRINT#4,"HELLO":CLOSE 4`.

## 6502/6510 Assembly

Assembly is used for maximum performance and control. For more information see `data/assembly/assembly-spec.md`.

- Addressing modes: `#imm, zp, zp,X, zp,Y, abs, abs,X, abs,Y, (zp), (zp,X), (zp),Y, rel`.
- Key opcodes (full set):
  - Load/Store: `LDA LDX LDY` / `STA STX STY`.
  - ALU: `ADC SBC AND ORA EOR ASL LSR ROL ROR`.
  - Inc/Dec: `INC INX INY DEC DEX DEY`.
  - Compare/Bit: `CMP CPX CPY BIT`.
  - Branch: `BCC BCS BEQ BMI BNE BPL BVC BVS`.
  - Jump/Call: `JMP JSR RTS RTI`.
  - Status: `CLC SEC CLI SEI CLD SED CLV NOP`.
  - Stack: `PHA PHP PLA PLP TAX TXA TAY TYA TSX TXS BRK`.
- Directives (assembler used here): `.org/*=`, `.byte`, `.word`, `.text/.ascii`, `ds` (fill), labels `name:`.
- Interrupts: set IRQ vector at $0314/$0315 to your routine; acknowledge VIC-II IRQ by writing back bit to $D019.
- Example (border flash): write to `$D020` inside raster IRQ (`$D012`/`$D011`), mask `$D01A`, acknowledge `$D019`.

## Context & RAG

- Layers: `data/context/bootstrap.md` → `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` / `.github/copilot-instructions.md` → `.github/prompts/*.prompt.md` → `.github/skills/*/SKILL.md` → `data/context/chat.md` → RAG docs (`doc/**/*.md`, `data/**/*.md`).

## 4. VIC bank and `$01` choices
| VIC bank | `$DD00` bits 0-1 | Range | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `%11` | `$0000-$3FFF` | default; char ROM seen at `$1000-$1FFF`; small games |
| 1 | `%10` | `$4000-$7FFF` | free of ROM images; good for bitmap games |
| 2 | `%01` | `$8000-$BFFF` | char ROM seen at `$9000-$9FFF` |
| 3 | `%00` | `$C000-$FFFF` | best for large games: code `$0800-$BFFF` stays contiguous |
- Keep other `$DD00` bits unchanged (read-modify-write). `$DD02` bits 0-1 must stay outputs. Inside the bank: `$D018` high nibble = screen (x `$400`), bits 1-3 = charset (x `$800`). Sprite pointers at `screen+$3F8`, value x 64 = offset in the bank.
- `$01`: `$37` BASIC+KERNAL+I/O (default), `$36` BASIC off, `$35` only I/O (typical game state: RAM `$A000-$BFFF`, `$E000-$FFFF`), `$34` all RAM (I/O hidden; toggle to `$35` for hardware access; IRQ handler must set `$35` itself), `$31`/`$33` expose char ROM for copying.
- With KERNAL off the vectors at `$FFFA/$FFFE` are RAM: set NMI (point to an `rti`, or a handler) and IRQ yourself; the `$0314` vector is no longer used. Keep CIA IRQs off (`$DC0D=$7F`, `$DD0D=$7F`, then read both).
- RAM under I/O (`$D000-$DFFF`) is visible to the VIC in bank 3 (sprite shapes, second charset): write it once at boot with `$01=$34`. Colour RAM `$D800` is separate, 4-bit, CPU-visible only with I/O on.

### A. Stock 64 KB game (AUTHENTIC; also valid MODERN), VIC bank 3, KERNAL off after boot
| Range | Use |
|---|---|
| `$0002-$008F` | zero page: hot variables, pointers, multiplexer order table (keep `$00/$01`; `$90-$FF` is free for the game once the KERNAL is off) |
| `$0100-$01FF` | stack |
| `$0200-$03FF` | small tables, IRQ trampolines, inter-program selector bytes (keep `$0314/5` untouched if KERNAL stays on) |
| `$0400-$07FF` | spare / loader scratch |
| `$0801` | BASIC stub `SYS` to start; code from `$0810` |
| `$0900-$8FFF` | code, tables, page-aligned hot data (about 32 KB) |
| `$9000-$9FFF` | level data window / decompression buffer |
| `$A000-$BFFF` | music + player, or more code/data (needs `$01<=$36`) |

| `$C800-$CFFF` | game charset |
| `$D000-$DFFF` | RAM under I/O: sprite shapes (up to 64) and/or second charset |
| `$E000-$FFFF` | bitmap, or 128 sprite shapes, or tile data; vectors at `$FFFA-$FFFF` |
Check: sprite shape addresses must be multiples of 64 and pointer value (addr-bank)/64 <= 255.

## 1. Raster IRQ and IRQ chains
Setup with KERNAL off (`$01=$35`; hardware vectors used):
```
        sei
        lda #$35
        sta $01
        lda #$7f          ; CIA IRQ sources off
        sta $dc0d
        sta $dd0d
        lda $dc0d         ; acknowledge pending
        lda $dd0d
        lda #<nmi
        sta $fffa
        lda #>nmi
        sta $fffb
        lda #<irq_top
        sta $fffe
        lda #>irq_top
        sta $ffff
        lda #$1b          ; bit 7 = raster line bit 8 = 0
        sta $d011
        lda #50
        sta $d012
        lda #$01          ; VIC raster IRQ on (enable last)
        sta $d01a
        lda #$ff
        sta $d019
        cli
main:   jmp main          ; main loop; never fall through into nmi
nmi:    rti
irq_top: pha
        txa
        pha
        tya
        pha
        lda #$ff          ; ack all VIC sources
        sta $d019
        ; ... work ...
        lda #<irq_next    ; chain: next vector and line
        sta $fffe
        lda #>irq_next
        sta $ffff
        lda #200
        sta $d012
        pla
        tay
        pla
        tax
        pla
        rti
```
- With KERNAL on use `$0314/$0315` and exit via `jmp $ea81` (skips keyboard scan) or `jmp $ea31`.
- Lines above 255: set `$D011` bit 7 for that entry (the 9th raster bit). Always rewrite `$D011` with bit 7 matching the next line.
- Chain rules: entries sorted by line; handler worst-case time shorter than the gap to the next entry; if the next line has already passed when you program `$D012`, run the next handler directly instead of waiting a whole frame; acknowledge `$D019` first; save `$01` if the main loop changes it. NMI must have a vector (RESTORE key).
- Decimal flag is not cleared on interrupt on the NMOS 6510: use `cld` in any handler that touches arithmetic.
- Latency: IRQ entry takes 7 cycles plus the instruction in progress (0-7 more), so the first line of a handler jitters by up to 7 cycles. Bad lines add up to 40 cycles of CPU stall (see architecture).
- Stable raster (needed for cycle-exact colour bars, border opening, hi-res tricks): the double-IRQ method. IRQ 1 fires on line N, installs IRQ 2 for line N+1, saves SP (`tsx`), enables interrupts (`cli`) and runs a NOP sled; IRQ 2 fires during a NOP, so jitter drops to 0-1 cycles; it restores SP (`txs`), burns cycles to the end of the line, and compares `$D012` twice to remove the last cycle (`lda $d012; cmp $d012; beq +`). Exact cycle counts depend on sprites and bad lines on that line; tune with a border-colour change and capture (`capture_frame`). Sketch only (unverified).
- MODERN: raster-exact code tuned for 1 MHz cycle counts is not cycle-exact in real time under turbo; keep cycle-critical effects at 1 MHz or measure on hardware. Prefer effects that need only line accuracy (scroll split, charset switch, colour changes).
- Sprites reused below another sprite, status-bar splits, `$D018`/`$D016` switches all hang on this chain.
**Seen in:** Oscar64 `rasterirq.h` library (IRQ chain with register-write lists), Tony (raster "copper" list), Cadaver multiplexer (hand-rolled precomputed chain).

## 5. Input
Joystick port 2: `$DC00`, port 1: `$DC01`; bits 0-4 = up, down, left, right, fire; 0 = pressed.
```
        lda $dc00         ; port 2
        eor #$ff          ; 1 = pressed
        and #$1f
        sta joy_cur
        eor joy_prev      ; changed bits
        and joy_cur       ; newly pressed this frame (edge)
        sta joy_edge
        lda joy_cur
        sta joy_prev
```
- Read once per frame at a fixed point (frame start). Use `joy_edge` for menu moves and jumps, `joy_cur` for movement; for auto-repeat count frames held.
- Port 1 (`$DC01`) shares lines with keyboard scanning; a pressed key shows up as joystick-1 input. Prefer port 2 for play; for port 1 write `$FF` to `$DC00` before reading and accept the conflict.
- Keyboard in games: scan the matrix (write a column mask to `$DC00`, read rows from `$DC01`) at a fixed time; the KERNAL's current-key byte `$CB` (64 = none) works only while the KERNAL IRQ runs. Use KERNAL `GETIN` (`$FFE4`) only in menus and name entry. Ghosting limits simultaneous keys.
- Accept joystick and keyboard together.
- Testing: `c64_input` `joystick` drives the game from the bridge; physical matrix injection (`machine:input`) is availability-dependent, check `c64://platform/status`.
- Paddles and the 1351 mouse use SID `$D419/$D41A` and the port-select bits of `$DC00` (unverified details); keep them optional.
**Seen in:** Tetris C64 (controlled-input module), Oscar64 samples (per-frame joystick polling and debounce), SquareDoom (1351 mouse option).

## 6. Music and sound effects
- PSID files (GoatTracker, SID-Wizard, other trackers export them) carry load, init and play addresses (`c64://sound/sid/file-format`). Place the player at its load address (often `$1000`); call `init` with the song number in A once; call `play` once per frame from the raster IRQ at a fixed line. If play address is 0 the tune installs its own interrupt: do not call it.
- Reserve the player's zero-page bytes and RAM range in the memory map before you write code. A player at `$A000-$BFFF` works when `$01<=$36`.
- Speed: a tune written for 50 Hz runs 20% fast at 60 Hz. On NTSC skip one call in six:
```
        dec tick
        bpl +
        lda #5
        sta tick
        bne skip          ; skip this frame's play call
+       jsr play          ; (tick counts 5..0, so one in six frames is skipped)
skip:
```
  Multi-speed tunes call `play` 2-4 times per frame from a CIA timer: handle with a timer IRQ instead of the frame IRQ (unverified for each player).
- SFX: SID has 3 voices. Common approach: dedicate voice 3 to SFX; after `jsr play` each frame, if an effect is active write its frequency/pulse/ADSR/control into voice 3 (`$D40E-$D414`) from an effect table (one step per frame); when the effect ends write control with gate off and let the music player take the voice again at its next note. Alternative: a player with built-in SFX support. Keep a priority byte so a weak effect never cuts a strong one.
- Volume `$D418` is shared and also holds filter mode: write it once per frame in one place.
- MODERN: more SIDs may exist at other addresses: put SFX on a second SID only after detecting that it is distinct and audible (`c64://ultimate/hardware`), with voice-stealing fallback. Digitised audio can come from REU (`c64://ultimate/reu`).
- SID writes during bad lines: fine, but avoid long write bursts mid-frame under turbo when SID sockets are used (accesses run at 1 MHz).
**Seen in:** Tetris C64 (`LoadSid`, init/play from frame code), Tony (player in `$A000-$BFFF`), Oscar64 `sidfx` sound effects.

## 8. PAL / NTSC timing
- Detect once at start. Quick: KERNAL flag `$02A6` (1 = PAL) set at KERNAL reset, valid if you did not overwrite it. Robust (derived from the line counts, test both models in VICE): PAL has 312 lines (max `$D012` seen above 255 is `$37`), NTSC 262 or 263 lines (max `$06`).
```
detect: lda $d011
        bpl detect        ; wait until raster line >= 256
chk:    lda $d012
        cmp #$10
        bcs is_pal        ; saw a line number >= 272
        bit $d011
        bmi chk           ; still above line 255
        lda #0            ; wrapped to line 0: NTSC
        rts
is_pal: lda #1
        rts
```
- Consequences: frame budget (architecture), music speed (above), IRQ lines for the bottom border and the maximum visible lines, sprite Y ranges (visible area differs by a few lines), colour palette differences, game speed (use frame counters scaled by a speed table; PAL 50 Hz vs NTSC about 60 Hz).
- MODERN: the Ultimate "System Mode" setting can select PAL, NTSC, PAL-60 or NTSC-50; detect at run time, never from the product name. `c64://ultimate/hardware`.
**Seen in:** common practice; see `c64://graphics/vic/spec` for line and cycle numbers.

### Sprite Pointer Configuration

Sprites are enabled via VIC-II registers:

- `$D015` - Sprite enable (bits 0-7 for sprites 0-7)
- `$D010` - Sprite X MSB for horizontal positioning beyond 255
- `$D000-$D00F` - X/Y coordinates for sprites 0-7
- `$07F8-$07FF` - Sprite data pointers (screen memory + $03F8)

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Memory Bandwidth and VIC-II Cycles -->
### Memory Bandwidth and VIC-II Cycles

**VIC-II "bad lines"** (every 8th raster, lines $30-$F7):

- VIC-II fetches 40 bytes of screen data + 40 bytes of character data
- CPU halted for ~40-43 cycles (exact depends on sprite activity)
- Bad lines occur when lower 3 bits of $D011 match lower 3 bits of raster counter

**Sprite DMA cycles**:

- Each active sprite costs 2 cycles per raster line for data fetch
- Sprite X-coordinate at DMA fetch point determines if CPU is blocked
- 8 sprites active: CPU loses 16 cycles per line
- Sprite display starts at cycle 11-12 of raster line

**Border timing and precision**:

- Upper border: Open at raster $30 by writing $D011 bit 3=0 at cycle 56
- Lower border: Open at raster $F7 by writing $D011 bit 3=1 at cycle 56  
- Side borders: $D016 bit 3 controls, must write at precise X-coordinate
- **NOP instruction** ($EA): Used for cycle-exact timing delays in border opening routines
- Typical pattern: `NOP; NOP; STA $D011` to hit exact cycle 56

**CPU availability**:

- Normal line: ~63 cycles available
- Bad line + 8 sprites: ~20 cycles available
- Critical code: Use raster lines outside $30-$F7 range or disable screen ($D011 bit 4=0)

## Practical Tips (LLM prompts → actions)

- **Reserve safe RAM** above BASIC: lower `MEMSIZ` ($37/$38) then `CLR` to keep ML/sprite/charset. RS‑232 OPEN auto‑lowers top by 512 for 2×256‑byte buffers.  
- **Dynamic keyboard**: preload KEYD ($0277–$0280), set NDX ($00C6), characters are consumed in order; handy for quoted INPUT.  
- **ROM banking** via $0001: temporarily map out BASIC/KERNAL/CHAR for patching or ROM reads; remember to **disable IRQs** before switching out KERNAL.  
- **Cassette buffer reuse**: if device 1 not active, use $033C–$03FB for short ML stubs or graphics data; keep header semantics in mind; **do not** run tape I/O concurrently.

### (A) Commodore BASIC Equivalent in Assembly

```asm
; Print "HELLO" to printer device #4 via KERNAL

    lda #4       ; Device number (printer)
    ldx #0       ; Secondary address
    ldy #1       ; Logical file number
    jsr $ffba    ; SETLFS

    lda #<msg
    ldx #>msg
    ldy #5       ; Length of message
    jsr $ffbd    ; SETNAM

    jsr $ffc0    ; OPEN
    lda #1
    jsr $ffc9    ; CHKOUT (select output channel)

    ldx #0
next:
    lda msg,x
    jsr $ffd2    ; CHROUT (send character)
    inx
    cpx #5
    bne next

    jsr $ffcc    ; CLRCHN (restore I/O)
    lda #1
    jsr $ffc3    ; CLOSE
    rts

msg: .text "HELLO"
```

Display conditions (`COND_MASK` bit): 0 screen on with badlines, 1 screen blanked (`$D011` bit 4 clear), 2 screen on plus
8 double-height sprites, 3 blanked plus 8 sprites. Loads (`VAR_MASK` bit): 0 RAM reads, 1 `sta $D020`, 2 `lda $D012`,
3 `lda $DC05` (CIA). Each loop pass is 48 cycles at 1 MHz: six times (one 4-cycle access plus two NOPs), so half of
the cycles are the chosen access. The unrolled loop is aligned to a page (a taken branch across a page costs one extra
cycle; this showed up as a 1.85 percent error in the first VICE validation run and is the reason for `.align 256`).

<!-- Source: data/ultimate/bench/README.md#Method -->
## Method

* Interrupts off (`sei`, CIA and VIC interrupt sources masked), `$01 = $35`, KERNAL and BASIC banked out.
* The clock is CIA2 timer A (PHI2 ticks) chained to timer B, 32 bits. PHI2 does not change with CPU speed, so the tick
  count is wall time in 1 MHz cycles.
* Each run synchronises to a raster line, starts the timers, executes a fixed number of passes `N = 29 x speed in MHz`
  (about 20 PAL frames, 0.4 s), and stops the timers. The speed is written through `$D031` (index | `BADBIT`).
  Start line differs per repetition (`$F8`, `$60`, `$A0`) so a phase effect against the badline pattern would show as spread.
* `$D031` is written repeatedly until a probe loop runs faster than 1 MHz (the firmware ignores the register for a
  while after a reset). Attempts per index are in the header (`$FF` = never took effect).
* Three frame-length measurements (raster line `$F8` to `$F8`) are stored. They must read 19656 (PAL) or 17095 (NTSC)
  plus or minus 7 and prove the timebase and synchronisation.
* Interference check: if the repetitions of a point differ by more than 0.78 percent the point gets flag 1. Reading
  C64 memory over REST pauses the CPU; a read during a run shows up here. The reported value is the median of the repetitions.

A "raw timer record" is 4 bytes: A low, A high, B low, B high of the CIA2 counters, which started at `$FFFF`:
`ticks = (0xFFFF - B) x 65536 + (0xFFFF - A)` (PHI2 cycles). Because of the counting convention the frame length reads
1 more than the nominal value for a perfectly aligned run (19657 against 19656).

* cpu records: record address = `$C300 + idx x 192 + cond x 48 + load x 12 + rep x 4`. All-zero bytes where a point
  was not selected by a mask.
* reu records: address = `$C300 + idx x 144 + cond x 72 + rep x 24 + transfer x 4`, cond 0 screen on, 1 blanked,
  transfer 0 stash 32 KB, 1 stash 16 KB, 2 stash 1 byte, 3 fetch 32 KB, 4 fetch 16 KB, 5 fetch 1 byte.
* window records: attempt k (0-based) at `$C300 + 8k`: probe timer record (4 bytes, probe ticks below 65536 means the
  probe ran faster than 1 MHz), then the free-running wall clock since program start (4 bytes, same encoding, ticks).

# Turbo benchmark results

Measured 2026-11-13 with `scripts/turbo-bench.mjs --suite full` (programs and method: `data/ultimate/bench/README.md`).
Raw decoded data, including every repetition's CIA tick count, is in `ultimate-64-2026-11-13.json` and `c64u-2026-11-13.json`.
Both machines were PAL, with the REU enabled (16 MB), interrupts off, `$01 = $35`. The frame-length records read 19657 ticks
(nominal 19656 plus the timer counting convention) in every run, which proves the timebase and raster synchronisation.

Definitions. "Multiple" is the delivered CPU rate as a multiple of PHI2 (0.985248 MHz PAL), so index 0 is 1.0000 and a
"48 MHz" setting is 47.00. "MHz" columns are multiple x 0.985248. "Cycles/frame" is the number of CPU cycles the program
executed per PAL frame, counted at the delivered speed (multiple x 19656 PHI2 cycles). "on" is the screen on with badlines
(`$D011 = $1B`), "blank" has `$D011` bit 4 clear, "+sprites" has eight double-height sprites enabled. Loads use 50 percent
accesses of the named type: `lda abs` from RAM, `sta $D020`, `lda $D012` (VIC), `lda $DC05` (CIA). Median of three repetitions,
three start rasters. `$D031` bit 7 clear (stock badline timing) in the main tables. REU rates are bytes per microsecond
(bytes per PHI2 tick x 0.985248), from the slope between 32 KB and 16 KB transfers.

Findings.

records.name: data/ultimate/bench/results/summary.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/bench/results/summary.md#Turbo benchmark results -->
* RAM speed scales with the setting: the blanked RAM multiple equals the nominal MHz up to 32 MHz on both machines, and is one
  short at the top entries (U64 idx 14/15: 38.99 and 47.00 for 40 and 48 MHz; C64U idx 14/15: 47.00 and 63.00 for 48 and
  64 MHz; C64U 40 MHz: 39.99).
* Screen on at 1 MHz loses 1081 cycles per PAL frame (25 badlines x 43.2); at higher speed the loss scales with the speed
  (about 5.5 percent at every index). Eight double-height sprites on a blanked screen cost another 802 cycles at 1 MHz,
  also scaling (4.1 percent).
* `$D031` bit 7 set removes all of that: screen on and blanked, with and without sprites, give the same multiple at 1, 12/14 and
  top speed (a loss of at most 0.2 percent remains at top speed). Bit 7 set means badline (and sprite) stalls are
  suppressed. The `Badline Timing` configuration item had no effect on results while Turbo Control was in registers mode
  (the program writes bit 7 through `$D031`); it was not tested separately in the other modes.
* Reading `$D012` falls behind RAM from 24 MHz and clearly from 32 MHz (U64 at 48 MHz: 42.1 against 47.0 multiples of PHI2;
  C64U at 64 MHz: 56.5 against 63.0). Writes to `$D020` run at RAM speed. A loop that reads a CIA register saturates: about
  4.0 multiples at 5-6 MHz, 7.5 at 8-12 MHz and 8.8 from 14 MHz up (the CPU waits for the CIA).
* REU DMA is not proportional to the CPU speed and is not monotonic. At 1, 2 and 3 MHz it is 1, 2 and 3 bytes per PHI2
  tick. The U64 stash is 3.0 to 5.1 B/us from 6 MHz up and the fetch 2.0 to 3.6 B/us (index 3 fetch equals index 1, index 5
  stash equals index 2); the C64U stash reaches 7.8 B/us and the fetch 4.3 B/us (stash at 10 MHz and 20 MHz is lower than at the
  neighbouring settings). With the screen on and badlines the rate is about 5 percent lower.
* After the reset done by `run_prg`, a `$D031` speed request was ignored for 2.55 s (U64) and 2.57 s (C64U) after program start.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/hardware.md#Turbo (CPU speed) -->
Timing facts:
- CPU and memory run at 48/64 MHz; the index chooses how many sub-slots per phi2 the CPU gets. VIC-II keeps priority, so graphics stay correct at any speed. CIA, VIC raster and SID stay in C64 time.
- Measured (PAL, screen blanked, RAM loop; measured 2026-11-13 on Ultimate 64 Elite fw 3.15a and C64U fw 1.2.1; rerun: c64://ultimate/hardware#rerun): the CPU gets the setting minus one VIC sub-slot at the top entries: 47 cycles per phi2 at 48 MHz (2,961 per PAL line), 63 at 64 MHz (3,969 per line, 1,238,387 per frame); exact up to 32 MHz. Cycles per PAL frame at 48 / 64 MHz: blanked 923,875 / 1,238,387; screen on 873,784 / 1,170,907; screen on plus 8 double-height sprites 836,375 / 1,121,520. At 1 MHz: 19,656 / 18,575 / 17,783. Badlines cost 5.5% at every speed, 8 sprites a further 4.1%. With `$D031` bit 7 set the screen-on loss is below 0.2% at every speed. `Badline Timing` had no effect in registers mode.
- I/O is slower than RAM at high speed: `lda $D012` gives 42 of 47 at 48 MHz and 56.5 of 63 at 64 MHz, `sta $D020` runs at RAM speed, a CIA read loop is capped near 8.8 (7.5 at 8-12 MHz). `sta abs,x` to I/O performs a dummy read and costs extra.
- Accesses to the external bus (cartridge port, real SID sockets) go through a 1 MHz bridge and wait for BA high. UltiSID writes are internal and fast.
- IEC bit-banging and cycle-counted raster tricks tuned for 1 MHz break under turbo.
- Forced 1 MHz window: after the reset done by `run_prg` a `$D031` request took effect 2.55 s (Elite 3.15a) and 2.57 s (C64U 1.2.1) after program start (measured); can recur briefly with IEC activity. Wait for it before timing-critical code.
- Measuring real speed (no register reports MHz): with interrupts off, time a fixed-cycle loop against `$D012` or CIA2 timers (PHI2 ticks). Accept only when two consecutive loops agree, rewrite `$D031` and retry during the 1 MHz window, give up after a bounded number of tries. The benchmark programs do this.
- Registers are not UCI. Turbo Control may be loaded from a `.cfg` named like the PRG (same folder, run from the Ultimate file browser) or applied by UCI LOAD_CONFIG (c64://ultimate/uci).
- Do not require turbo; provide a 1 MHz path and a text message naming the setting.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/reu.md#Registers (`$DF00-$DF0A`) -->
## Registers (`$DF00-$DF0A`)

| Addr | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `$DF00` | Status (R) | b7 IRQ pending, b6 END OF BLOCK, b5 FAULT (verify mismatch), b4 size >= 256 KB (not a size probe), b3-0 version. **Reading clears b6, b5 and the IRQ**: read once, keep a copy. |
| `$DF01` | Command | b7 EXECUTE, b5 AUTOLOAD, b4 FF00 (1 = run at once, 0 = wait for a write to `$FF00`), b1-0 type: 00 stash (C64 to REU), 01 fetch (REU to C64), 10 swap, 11 verify |
| `$DF02/03` | C64 address lo/hi | reads return the advancing address |
| `$DF04/05/06` | REU address lo/mid/bank | bank = 64 KB units |
| `$DF07/08` | Length lo/hi | 0 = 65536 bytes; reads return remaining count |
| `$DF09` | IRQ mask | b7 enable, b6 on END OF BLOCK, b5 on FAULT |
| `$DF0A` | Address control | b7 fix C64 address, b6 fix REU address (not cleared by transfers) |

Command bytes: `$90` stash, `$91` fetch, `$92` swap, `$93` verify (execute, immediate, no autoload); `$B0-$B3` same with autoload; `$80-$83` wait for `$FF00` write.
- Without autoload, after a transfer both base addresses point past the last byte and length reads 1: consecutive blocks can continue without rewriting REU address, but length and C64 address must be set again as needed. With autoload the base values are restored (repeat the same transfer with only `$DF01`).
- Swap: both memories read, then both written. Verify: stops at first mismatch, FAULT set, END OF BLOCK not set; the address registers point at the mismatching byte on Ultimate devices (real REUs differ). Clear FAULT first by reading `$DF00`.
- C64 address wraps at `$FFFF`. `$DF0A = $80` (fix C64 address): a fetch writes every REU byte to one location, at DMA speed (too fast to play samples). `$40` (fix REU address): a fetch fills memory with one byte.
- Write all bytes of a base-address pair before executing.
- Extended registers on some FPGA builds (existence on U64/C64U cores unverified): `$DF0C` size mask (`$01` 128 KB ... `$FF` 16 MB), `$DF0D` start delay, `$DF0E` rate divider, `$DF0F` length bits 23-16 (write-only, allows over 64 KB per transfer). Probe `$DF0C` before use; do not depend on it.
- `$DF1B-$DF1F` are UCI (the REU logic aliases `$DF10-$DF1F`): use only `$DF00-$DF0A`.

records.name: data/ultimate/reu.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/reu.md#Timing, stall, size, wrap -->
- The CPU is halted for the whole transfer (no wait loop needed; the status is valid on the next instruction). A raster/CIA IRQ falling inside it fires late. Menu freeze pauses a running transfer.
- Measured 2026-11-13 on Ultimate 64 Elite fw 3.15a and C64U fw 1.2.1, PAL, 16 MB REU; rerun: c64://ultimate/hardware#rerun or c64://ultimate/bench. The rate depends on the CPU turbo setting (1 byte per microsecond holds only at 1-3 MHz). Bytes per microsecond, stash / fetch, screen blanked: 1 MHz 0.99 / 0.99, 2 MHz 1.97 / 1.97, 3 MHz 2.96 / 2.93. Top speed: U64 48 MHz 5.1 / 3.6, C64U 64 MHz 7.8 / 4.3. Not monotonic: U64 4 MHz fetch 2.0 and 6 MHz stash 3.0; C64U 10 MHz stash 4.9 against 7.7 at 8 MHz. Floors from 6 MHz up: U64 3.0 / 2.6, C64U 4.9 / 2.9.
- Screen on with badlines costs about 5 percent of the rate;none with `$D031` bit 7 set. Each transfer has a fixed overhead of 3 to 15 PHI2 ticks (1-byte transfers: 15 at 1 MHz, 3 at top speed).
- At top speed a CPU store loop (derived: about 12 B/us at 64 MHz) outruns REU stash: do not DMA-fill then.
- **512 KB wrap:** on builds without the extended registers, and in VICE, a transfer that crosses a 512 KB boundary (REU address multiple of `$080000`) wraps inside that block. Rule: split every DMA so `(addr & $07FFFF) + len <= $080000`; guard length 0 (it means 64 KB). Extended builds mask the address to the configured size instead.
- **Size detection** (no UCI command reports it): fetch the byte at REU offset 0, stash back `a^$A5`, fetch again (no REU if it does not hold; restore it). Then for s = 64 KB, 128 KB, ... 8 MB: save bytes at 0 and s, write `a^$A5` at 0 and `a^$5A` at s; if offset 0 now holds the second value the REU aliases at s, so size = s. Restore the bytes. No wrap up to 8 MB means 16 MB. Also verify a magic header and block checksums after loading: a missing or stale REU returns valid-looking stale data without error.
- **`$FF00` trigger** (b4 = 0): set the command, change `$01` (e.g. to `$34` for RAM under I/O), then store to `$FF00`. Whether this reaches RAM under I/O on the C64U is unverified; the safe route is DMA into a normal-RAM bounce buffer then CPU copy. DMA writes to colour RAM (`$D800`) need I/O visible.
- Turbo: starting a transfer must halt the CPU in the same cycle as the `$DF01` write. Firmware before 2026-08-28 could run instructions after the command write while DMA was in flight on U64-class cores. Put no instruction after `sta $DF01` that depends on the transfer or on stable REU registers, add `nop nop`, and disable interrupts from first register write to the trigger.

| Addr | Read | Write |
|---|---|---|
| `$DF1B` | SoftwareIEC device number (0 unset) | - |
| `$DF1C` | Status | Control (bits are commands) |

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/uci.md#Exchange -->
## Exchange

1. Wait STATE = idle. 2. Write command bytes to `$DF1D` (target first). 3. Write `$01` to `$DF1C`. 4. Poll until STATE leaves busy. 5. Read `$DF1E` while DATA_AV, then `$DF1F` while STAT_AV. 6. Write `$02`. data-last returns to idle; data-more returns to busy for another block (back to 4).

- Never read-modify-write `$DF1C` (reads return status, not control). No `inc`/`ora`/`asl` on it.
- Use absolute addressing for UCI/REU registers (indexed stores do a dummy read).
- No data phase (state goes busy then idle): REBOOT, a zero-length command, and any command whose first byte has bit 7 set (no-reply flag, e.g. `$84 $05`). Do not wait for a data state.
- Target = first byte `& $0F`. Second byte = command; `$01` is IDENTIFY on every target. Unimplemented targets answer IDENTIFY with `NO TARGET` and any other command with `21,UNKNOWN COMMAND`.
- Limits: command 895 bytes, response block 895, status 255. A reply that exactly fills a queue leaves DATA_AV set forever: bound every read loop.
- Strings need no terminator. Names and URLs are ASCII: convert from PETSCII (cc65 literals arrive case-swapped).
- Stuck interface (data-more after an abandoned read): write `$02` until STATE < data-last, then `$04`, then `$08`. Do this at startup too (a crashed program can leave half-written command bytes).
- Nothing is timed: use bounded poll loops (200x256 polls is about 1.5 s at 1 MHz; network/HTTP need far longer; scale with turbo).
- One command in flight; an IRQ handler may run but must not use UCI. During SoftwareIEC loads, REU DMA and U64_SAVEMEM the machine is halted (music and raster IRQs stop).
- A C64 reset releases network sockets but not HTTP handles or (probably) the DOS file: on startup ABORT, close the DOS file, FREE_ALL HTTP.

<!-- Source: data/ultimate/uci.md#Minimal 6502 routine (ca65 syntax, fresh example) -->
## Minimal 6502 routine (ca65 syntax, fresh example)

```
UCI_CTRL = $DF1C        ; write
UCI_STAT = $DF1C        ; read
UCI_CMD  = $DF1D
UCI_ID   = $DF1D
UCI_RESP = $DF1E
UCI_SDAT = $DF1F
; zp cmdp -> command bytes; rbuf, sbuf = reply buffers (255 bytes max)

; presence: lda UCI_ID / and #$7F / cmp #$49 (Z set = present)
uci_cmd:                ; X = command length (1..255); returns A = final STATE bits
@idle:  lda UCI_STAT    ;  add a timeout in real code
        and #$30
        bne @idle
        ldy #0
@send:  lda (cmdp),y
        sta UCI_CMD
        iny
        dex
        bne @send
        lda #$01        ; literal PUSH_CMD
        sta UCI_CTRL
@busy:  lda UCI_STAT
        and #$30
        cmp #$10
        beq @busy
        ldy #0          ; response bytes, bounded at 255
@rd:    lda UCI_STAT
        bpl @st         ; bit 7 clear: no data
        lda UCI_RESP
        sta rbuf,y
        iny
        bne @rd
@st:    ldx #0
@sd:    lda UCI_STAT
        and #$40
        beq @done
        lda UCI_SDAT
        sta sbuf,x
        inx
        bne @sd
@done:  lda UCI_STAT
        and #$30        ; $20 data-last, $30 data-more, $00 no data phase
        pha
        lda #$02        ; DATA_ACC
        sta UCI_CTRL
        pla
        rts
```
Y after `@rd` is the byte count (0 = none or 256). For `$30` (more blocks) repeat from `@busy`. Example: `01 01` (DOS IDENTIFY) gives `ULTIMATE-II DOS V1.2`, status `00,OK`. Further reading: ultimate-uci-sdk (MIT).

### Machine

| Method | Path | Parameters | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:reset` | – | Sends a reset to the machine. Configuration remains unchanged. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:reboot` | – | Restarts the machine and re-initialises the cartridge configuration. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:pause` | – | Pulls the DMA line low at a safe moment, stopping the CPU while timers continue. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:resume` | – | Releases the DMA line so the CPU resumes execution. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:poweroff` | – | Powers off the machine. Responses are not guaranteed. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:menu_button` | – | Toggles the Ultimate menu just like the physical button. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:writemem` | `address`, `data` | Writes data to C64 memory through DMA using the currently selected memory map. Writing to 6510 I/O registers is not possible. Up to 128 bytes are written. |
| POST | `/v1/machine:writemem` | `address` | Writes attached binary data starting at the supplied address. The data must not wrap beyond `$FFFF`. |
| GET | `/v1/machine:readmem` | `address`, `[length]` | Performs a DMA read and returns binary data. The default length is 256 bytes. |
| GET | `/v1/machine:debugreg` | – | Reads `$D7FF` and returns the value field in hexadecimal. Ultimate 64 only. |
| PUT | `/v1/machine:debugreg` | `value` | Writes the hexadecimal value to `$D7FF`, then reads it back. Ultimate 64 only. |

Example for `/v1/machine:writemem`:

```text
PUT /v1/machine:writemem?address=D020&data=0504
```

This sequence writes `05` to `$D020` and `04` to `$D021`.

; hello_world_prg.asm
; Single-file PRG layout:
; - Tokenized one-line BASIC at $0801: 10 SYS 4096
; - Machine code placed at $1000 which writes the message directly to screen RAM ($0400)
;   (no KERNAL CHROUT or BASIC printing is used)

        .org $0801
        ; next-line pointer (little-endian) -> $080C (start + line length)
        .byte $0C, $08
        ; line number 10
        .byte $0A, $00
        ; tokenized content: SYS (0x9E), space (0x20), '4','0','9','6' (ASCII/PETSCII digits)
        .byte $9E, $20, $34, $30, $39, $36
        ; line terminator
        .byte $00
        ; program end marker (two zero bytes)
        .byte $00, $00

        ; -- machine code at $1000 ------------------------------------------------
        .org $1000
start:
        ldx #$00            ; X = 0
write_loop:
        lda message, x      ; load byte from message
        beq done            ; zero terminator -> finished
        sta $0400, x        ; write character to screen RAM (fast direct write)
        inx
        jmp write_loop

done:
        rts

message:
        ; ASCII bytes for: HELLO, WORLD!  (0-terminated)
        ; VIC-II screen codes for: HELLO, WORLD! (screen codes from data/graphics/character-set.csv)
        ; H E  L  L  O   ,    <space> W  O  R  L  D  !
        .byte $08, $05, $0C, $0C, $0F, $2C, $20, $17, $0F, $12, $0C, $04, $21, $00

        ; End of file
